catalog_quote: My recording of the following Basay is based on an old woman named Pan-rau Tzeng (曾潘蟯), who originally came from Shinshe, Gungliau (貢寮新社), where she picked up the following words in her childhood from an old Basay woman with gray hair. Stress falls on the final syllable. The stops and the affricate /c/ [ts] are generally unaspirate. The Kavalan forms cited after a few Basay forms for comparison below are also based on my own field notes. ... [p. 92:] Even in 1987, I was still able to collect 67 words and phrases for Basay from an 83 year-old woman living in Jilung. new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress falls on the final syllable (as observed in the 67 words and phrases Li recorded in 1987 from a rememberer of the Shinshe/Gungliau variety of Basay).
new_statements.exceptions: None stated; the author cautions that the informant was not a native speaker (words remembered from childhood), that phonetic details of the extinct language are imperfectly understood, and that pronunciation may be influenced by Taiwanese Southern Min; she may also have added a vowel [e] after final /c/ (fn. p. 93).
new_statements.domain_note: Isolated citation forms (elicited wordlist of 67 words/phrases); no discussion of phrase-level prosody. The only first-hand auditory observation of Basay stress in print that could be located; Asai's 1936 fieldnotes (the main Basay corpus) come with no phonetic description per Li 1999:481.
new_statements.identity_note: The statement concerns the Shinshe (貢寮新社, Gungliau, Taipei/Keelung coast) variety of Basay proper, i.e. basa1287, as remembered by a non-native rememberer recorded by Li in 1987 in Jilung (Keelung). It does not cover the Trobiawan dialect of Ilan (Asai's other informant), for which no stress statement was found.

sources.note: Sec. 2.1 Basay (reprint p. 93), introducing 67 words/phrases Li recorded in 1987 from an 83-year-old rememberer from Shinshe (Gungliau): 'Stress falls on the final syllable. The stops and the affricate /c/ [ts] are generally unaspirate.' (For comparison the same paper says Taokas 'Stress falls on the penult', p. 101.) Li cautions (p. 92) that phonetic details of these extinct languages are imperfectly understood and informants' pronunciation may be influenced by Taiwanese.

sources.note: Grammar sketch based on Asai's 1936 fieldnotes (Shinshe and Trobiawan dialects); phonology confined to a footnote (p. 481): 4 vowels, 14 consonants, geminates, 'Phonetic descriptions for these segments are unavailable.' No mention of stress or accent anywhere (scanned a full-text search for stress/accent: stress/accent/penult/syllable).
